node-di-container.title: Dependency injection: resolution order and cycles
node-di-container.description:
A dependency-injection container knows, for every service name, the list of services it needs: `registry = {name: [dependency, …]}`.
To build `target` it must first build each dependency (in the listed order, depth-first), and each service is built **once** (a singleton).

`resolveOrder(registry, target)` returns the list of service names in the order they are instantiated, ending with `target`.

Errors are returned as an object instead:
- a name that is not registered → `{error: "missing: <name>"}`;
- a dependency cycle → `{error: "cycle: a -> b -> c -> a"}`, listing the cycle from the service where it starts back to itself.

The first problem met during the depth-first walk is the one reported.

**Example:** `registry = {app:["db","logger"], db:["config","logger"], logger:["config"], config:[]}`, `target = "app"` → `["config","logger","db","app"]`.
With `{a:["b"], b:["c"], c:["a"]}` and target `"a"` → `{error:"cycle: a -> b -> c -> a"}`.

guide.prereqs: Recursion and depth-first search, `Set`. The lesson *Singleton, module wiring and dependency injection*.
guide.intuition: Getting dressed: socks before shoes. To put on an item, first put on everything it needs. If while dressing you find that the item you need is one you are *currently in the middle of* putting on, the instructions are circular. So track two things: finished items, and the chain in progress.
hints: Depth-first search that appends a name **after** visiting all its dependencies (post-order).
Keep `done` (a Set of finished services) and `stack` (the chain being built right now, an array).
If a name is already on the stack, the cycle is `stack.slice(indexOf(name))` plus the name again.
guide.brute_force: Repeatedly scan the registry for a service whose dependencies are all built: O(n²), and it cannot easily say *which* services form the cycle.
guide.approach:
`visit(name)`: done → skip; unregistered → missing; on stack → cycle; else push, visit deps, pop, mark done, append.

**Dry run** on the first example: visit `app` → `db` → `config` (no deps) → order `[config]`; back in `db` → `logger` → `config` done → order `[config, logger]`; `db` done → `[config, logger, db]`; back in `app`, `logger` already done; append `app`.
guide.complexity: O(V + E) visits; with `indexOf` on the stack the worst case is O(V·depth). Space O(V).
guide.pitfalls:
- Using one `visited` set for both purposes: a cycle then looks like an already-built service and a broken order is returned.
- Reporting the whole path from the target instead of the cycle only (`t -> a -> b -> a` should be `a -> b -> a`).
- Building a shared dependency twice.
guide.follow_up: Extend the container so each registration has a factory function and `resolve(name)` returns the built instance; add a `transient` lifetime that builds a fresh instance every time.

node-proxy.title: A validating, logging proxy
node-proxy.description:
Wrap a plain object (the *subject*) in a **proxy** that validates writes against a schema and records every successful access.

`schema` maps field names to a type name (`"number"`, `"string"` or `"boolean"`). The subject starts empty.
`runProxy(schema, ops)` performs the operations through the proxy and returns `{results, log, target}` where `target` is the subject at the end.

| operation | behaviour | result | log entry (only on success) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `["set", key, value]` | key not in schema → error; `typeof value` differs from the schema type → error; otherwise store | `true` | `set key=<JSON of value>` |
| `["get", key]` | key not in schema → error; otherwise read | the value, or `null` if not set | `get key` |
| `["has", key]` | is the field currently set? (any key is allowed) | `true`/`false` | `has key` |
| `["delete", key]` | remove the field if it is set | `true` if something was removed, else `false` | `delete key` (only when removed) |
| `["keys"]` | list the fields currently set, in insertion order | array of names | `keys` |

Errors do not stop the run: the result of the failing operation is the string `"error: unknown field <key>"` or `"error: <key> must be a <type>"`, and nothing is logged for it.

**Example:** schema `{age:"number"}`, ops `[["set","age","7"],["set","age",7],["get","age"],["get","name"]]`
→ results `["error: age must be a number", true, 7, "error: unknown field name"]`, log `["set age=7","get age"]`, target `{age:7}`.

Tip: JavaScript's built-in `Proxy` has traps named `get`, `set`, `has`, `deleteProperty` and `ownKeys`.

guide.prereqs: Objects, `typeof`, `try`/`catch`. The lesson *The proxy pattern*.
guide.intuition: A proxy is a receptionist in front of an office. Visitors talk to the receptionist exactly as they would to the office, but the receptionist checks badges (validation) and writes the visitor book (logging) before letting anything through. The office itself knows nothing about it.
hints: Create `new Proxy(target, handler)` and give `handler` the traps `get`, `set`, `has`, `deleteProperty`, `ownKeys`.
Throw an `Error` inside a trap for invalid access; catch it where you run each operation and turn it into the `"error: …"` string.
Log only after the checks have passed. Use `Object.hasOwn` rather than truthiness so `0`, `""` and `false` are real values.
guide.brute_force: Skip `Proxy` and write an `if` chain per operation. It passes the tests, but callers would then need a special API instead of ordinary property syntax, which is the thing the proxy pattern avoids.
guide.approach:
Traps do validation and logging; a small dispatcher maps each op to ordinary syntax on the proxy (`proxy[key] = value`, `proxy[key]`, `key in proxy`, `Reflect.deleteProperty`, `Object.keys`).

**Dry run** on the example: `set age "7"` → trap sees `typeof "7"` is `string`, schema wants `number` → throws → result is the error string, no log. `set age 7` passes → stored, logged `set age=7`. `get age` → logged, returns 7. `get name` → not in schema → error.
guide.complexity: O(1) per operation except `keys`, which is O(number of fields).
guide.pitfalls:
- Logging before validating.
- `target[key] || null` loses falsy values.
- A schema field called `toString`: check own properties, not inherited ones.
- In strict mode a `set` trap that returns `false` makes the assignment throw a `TypeError`; return `true` after storing.
guide.follow_up: Make the proxy *reactive*: call a callback with `(key, oldValue, newValue)` on every successful change, the mechanism behind several UI frameworks.

results: error: age must be a number
error: flag must be a boolean
error: flag must be a boolean
error: s must be a string

node-decorator.title: Stack decorators around a service
node-decorator.description:
A base service has one method, `get(key)`, which returns `data[key]`, or `null` when the key is absent. Every call that reaches the base service is counted in `baseCalls`.

**Decorators** wrap the service and offer the same `get(key)` method. `decorators` lists them from the **innermost** (applied first, closest to the base) to the **outermost**:

| name | what its `get` does |
|---|---|
| `"cache"` | remembers the result per key (including `null`) and does not call the inner service again for that key |
| `"upper"` | calls the inner service; upper-cases the result if it is a string |
| `"count"` | counts its own invocations, then calls the inner service |
| `"default:TEXT"` | calls the inner service; replaces a `null` result by `TEXT` |

Call the outermost `get` once for each entry of `keys`. Return `{results, baseCalls, counts}` where `counts` holds one number per `"count"` decorator, in the order they appear in `decorators`.

**Example:** `data = {a:"x"}`, `decorators = ["count","cache","count"]`, `keys = ["a","a","b","a"]`
→ `{results:["x","x",null,"x"], baseCalls:2, counts:[2,4]}` (the inner counter sits behind the cache and sees only the misses).

guide.prereqs: Closures, objects with methods, `Map`. The lesson *Decorator and adapter*.
guide.intuition: Decorators are layers of clothing on the same person: each layer adds one thing and passes everything else through to the layer underneath. Because every layer has the same shape as the service, layers can be stacked in any number and any order, and the order changes the outcome.
hints: Start with `let service = base` and, for each decorator name, replace `service` by a new object whose `get` calls the previous `service`.
Capture the previous service in a `const inner` inside the loop body so each layer keeps its own reference.
Use `Map.has` for the cache so a cached `null` counts as a hit; give each `count` layer its own slot in `counts`.
guide.brute_force: One big function with flags (`useCache`, `useUpper`, …). It cannot express two caches, three counters or a different order without more flags.
guide.approach:
Fold the decorator list over the base service, then call the result.

**Dry run** on the example (`count₀`, `cache`, `count₁` from inside out): `a` → count₁=1, cache miss → count₀=1 → base (1). `a` → count₁=2, hit. `b` → count₁=3, miss → count₀=2 → base (2) → `null`, cached. `a` → count₁=4, hit. `baseCalls 2`, `counts [2,4]`.
guide.complexity: O(layers) per call; O(distinct keys) memory per cache layer.
guide.pitfalls:
- Building the stack in the wrong direction.
- `var`/shared variables so that every layer points at the last service (infinite recursion).
- Treating `null` as "not cached".
guide.follow_up: The same idea decorates functions: `withRetry(withTimeout(fetchUser))`. Write `compose(...decorators)`.

node-adapter.title: Adapt a string store to a collection API
node-adapter.description:
You are given (in the starter) a tiny **string-only key-value store** with four methods: `setItem(key, value)`, `getItem(key)` (returns `null` when absent),
`removeItem(key)` and `keys()`. The rest of the application wants a **collection** interface instead. Write an **adapter** class that offers the collection
methods and implements them using *only* the store's methods.

| collection method | meaning | result |
|---|---|---|
| `add(item)` | store a plain object and give it the next id (1, 2, 3, …; ids are never reused) | the id |
| `find(id)` | fetch the object | the object, or `null` |
| `remove(id)` | delete the object | `true` if it existed, else `false` |
| `list()` | all objects in ascending id order, each with its id merged in: `{id, ...item}` | array |

Storage layout (this is checked): the item with id `n` lives under key `"item:n"` as `JSON.stringify(item)`; the last id handed out lives under key `"seq"` as a decimal string.
The key `"seq"` exists only after the first `add`.

`runAdapter(ops)` runs operations such as `["add", {name:"Ada"}]`, `["find", 1]`, `["remove", 1]`, `["list"]` and returns `{results, raw}` where `raw` is the store's final content.

**Example:** `[["add",{"name":"Ada"}],["add",{"name":"Lin"}],["remove",1],["list"]]`
→ `{results:[1,2,true,[{id:2,name:"Lin"}]], raw:{"seq":"2","item:2":"{\"name\":\"Lin\"}"}}`

guide.prereqs: Classes, `JSON.stringify`/`JSON.parse`, array sorting. The lesson *Decorator and adapter*.
guide.intuition: A travel plug: your laptop's plug does not change and neither does the wall socket; a small piece in between has one shape on each side. The adapter speaks "collection" to the application and "string store" to the storage.
hints: Each collection method is one or two calls on `this.storage`. Decide the key naming first: `"item:" + id` and `"seq"`.
`add`: read `seq` (missing means 0), add 1, write it back, write the JSON text.
`list`: take `keys()`, keep the `item:` ones, turn the suffix into a number, sort numerically, then `find` each.
guide.brute_force: Keep the objects in an array inside the adapter. It answers the calls but nothing reaches the store, so the data is lost on restart; that is not adapting, it is replacing.
guide.approach:
Translate method by method.

**Dry run** on the example: `add Ada` → seq `"1"`, `item:1 = {"name":"Ada"}` → 1. `add Lin` → seq `"2"`, `item:2` → 2. `remove 1` → key exists → removed → `true`. `list` → keys `seq`, `item:2` → ids `[2]` → `[{id:2, name:"Lin"}]`.
guide.complexity: `add`/`find`/`remove` O(1) store calls; `list` O(n log n) for n items.
guide.pitfalls:
- Deriving the next id from the number of items: ids get reused after a removal.
- Sorting ids as strings puts 10 before 2.
- Storing objects without `JSON.stringify` (the store would keep `"[object Object]"`).
guide.follow_up: Write a second adapter with the same collection interface on top of an array-of-rows store; the application code would not change at all.

node-strategy.title: Pluggable discount strategies
node-strategy.description:
A checkout computes a total from `items` (each `{price, qty}`, price in whole cents) using a **strategy** chosen by name. All amounts are integers.

Let `subtotal` be the sum of `price * qty`. A discount of `p` percent on an amount `x` gives `x - Math.round(x * p / 100)`.

| strategy | `param` | total |
|---|---|---|
| `"none"` | (ignored) | `subtotal` |
| `"percent"` | `{percent}` | the discount applied to the subtotal |
| `"bulk"` | `{min, percent}` | each line with `qty >= min` gets the discount applied to that line; other lines are full price |
| `"threshold"` | `{min, amount}` | if `subtotal >= min`, subtract `amount` (never below 0); otherwise `subtotal` |

Return `{subtotal, total}`, or `{error: "unknown strategy: <name>"}` for any other name.

**Example:** `checkout([{price:1000,qty:3},{price:250,qty:1}], "bulk", {min:3, percent:10})` → `{subtotal:3250, total:2950}`

guide.prereqs: `reduce`, objects holding functions. The lesson *Strategy, state and template*.
guide.intuition: A sat-nav with a "fastest / shortest / no motorways" switch: the trip (context) is the same, the rule for choosing the route is swapped. Here the context computes the subtotal and hands the pricing decision to whichever strategy function was selected.
hints: Compute `subtotal` once, outside the strategies.
Store the strategies in an object keyed by name; each is a function of `param` returning the total.
Look the name up with `Object.hasOwn` and return the error object if it is not there.
guide.brute_force: An `if`/`else if` chain inside `checkout`. It works, but each new discount rule edits the checkout function itself, which is what the pattern is meant to prevent.
guide.approach:
Table of functions.

**Dry run** on the example: subtotal `3000 + 250 = 3250`. `bulk` with min 3, 10%: line 1 has qty 3 → `3000 - 300 = 2700`; line 2 has qty 1 → `250`. Total `2950`.
guide.complexity: O(number of items).
guide.pitfalls:
- Applying the bulk discount to the whole cart instead of per line.
- `>` instead of `>=` at the threshold.
- A threshold discount larger than the subtotal producing a negative total.
- `table[name]` is truthy for `"constructor"`.
guide.follow_up: Let strategies be combined: accept a list of strategies and return the best total for the customer.

node-state-machine.title: A circuit breaker state machine
node-state-machine.description:
A **circuit breaker** protects a failing remote service from being hammered. It is a state machine with three states.

- **closed** (normal): requests go through. A failure adds 1 to a counter of *consecutive* failures; a success resets the counter to 0. When the counter reaches `threshold`, the breaker becomes **open** and remembers the time.
- **open**: requests are rejected immediately, without calling the service, while `t < openedAt + cooldown`. The first request with `t >= openedAt + cooldown` switches the breaker to **half-open** and is let through as a trial.
- **half-open**: the trial request decides. Success → **closed** with the counter at 0. Failure → **open** again, with `openedAt` set to this request's time.

`events` is a time-ordered list of `{t, ok}`: a request arrives at time `t`, and `ok` says whether the service *would* succeed if it is actually called.
Return `{results, state}`: one of `"ok"`, `"fail"`, `"rejected"` per event, and the state after the last event (`"closed"`, `"open"` or `"half-open"`).

**Example:** `threshold = 2`, `cooldown = 10`, events at t = 0 (fail), 1 (fail), 2 (ok), 11 (ok), 12 (ok)
→ `{results:["fail","fail","rejected","ok","ok"], state:"closed"}`

guide.prereqs: Loops and conditionals. The lesson *Strategy, state and template* (state section).
guide.intuition: A household fuse. Too many faults in a row and it trips: nothing flows, which protects the wiring. After a while you push it back in carefully (half-open): if the fault is gone it stays in; if not, it trips again at once.
hints: Keep three variables: `state`, the consecutive-failure counter and `openedAt`.
Handle `open` first: either reject and move on, or switch to `half-open` and fall through to the normal request handling.
On failure, the reaction depends on the state: half-open reopens immediately; closed increments the counter and compares with `threshold`.
guide.brute_force: No shortcut exists; you must process events in order. The naive mistake is to treat half-open as closed.
guide.approach:
Single pass with explicit transitions.

**Dry run** on the example (threshold 2, cooldown 10): t=0 fail → counter 1. t=1 fail → counter 2 → open at 1. t=2: `2 < 11` → rejected (the service would have succeeded, but it is never asked). t=11: `11 >= 11` → half-open, trial succeeds → closed. t=12 ok.
guide.complexity: O(number of events) time, O(1) state.
guide.pitfalls:
- Counting failures that are not consecutive.
- Using `>` instead of `>=` for the cooldown boundary.
- Updating `openedAt` on rejected requests, which would keep the breaker open forever under steady traffic.
guide.follow_up: In the lesson the same machine is written with one object per state, each implementing `request()`. Refactor your solution that way.

node-iterator.title: A lazy page-flattening iterator
node-iterator.description:
A paginated API returns `pages`: a list of pages, each a list of items (pages may be empty). Build an **iterator** that walks over all items, page by page,
without first copying them into one big array, and drive it with `ops`. Items are never `null`.

| operation | result |
|---|---|
| `["next"]` | `{done:false, value:item}` and advance; once everything is consumed, `{done:true, value:null}` (every time) |
| `["peek"]` | the item that the following `next` would return, without consuming it; `null` if exhausted |
| `["skip", n]` | consume up to `n` items; the result is how many were actually skipped |
| `["reset"]` | start again from the first item; result `null` |

Return the list of results.

**Example:** `pages = [[1,2],[],[3]]`, ops `[["next"],["peek"],["skip",5],["next"],["reset"],["next"]]`
→ `[{done:false,value:1}, 2, 2, {done:true,value:null}, null, {done:false,value:1}]`

guide.prereqs: Generators (`function*`, `yield`) or manual index bookkeeping. The lesson *Iterators, generators and async iterators*.
guide.intuition: A bookmark in a multi-volume book. `next` reads a line and moves the bookmark; `peek` reads the line and leaves the bookmark; pages without text are skipped over. The reader never needs to photocopy the whole book first.
hints: A generator with two nested `for...of` loops yields the items lazily and skips empty pages for free.
Generators cannot look ahead, so `peek` must fetch one result and park it in a variable that `next` checks first.
`reset` creates a fresh generator and clears the parked result. Compare with `done`, never with truthiness.
guide.brute_force: `pages.flat()` and an index. Correct and short, O(total items) memory; with a real paginated API you could not load all pages up front, which is why the lazy version matters.
guide.approach:
Generator plus one-slot look-ahead buffer.

**Dry run** on the example: `next` → 1. `peek` → pulls 2 into the buffer, returns 2. `skip 5` → consumes buffered 2, then 3, then hits the end → 2 skipped. `next` → done. `reset` → new generator. `next` → 1.
guide.complexity: O(1) amortised per consumed item, O(1) extra memory.
guide.pitfalls:
- `peek` advancing the position.
- Forgetting the buffered item when skipping or resetting.
- Treating `0`, `false` or `""` as "no more items".
guide.follow_up: Make it an *async* iterator where each page is fetched on demand: `for await (const item of iteratePages(fetchPage))`.

node-middleware-onion.title: Run a middleware chain (the onion model)
node-middleware-onion.description:
Web frameworks such as Koa run a request through a **stack of middleware**. Each middleware receives a `next` function; calling it runs the rest of the stack
(and finally the route handler) and then *returns*, so code after `next()` runs on the way back out. This is the onion model.

`runMiddleware(stack)` receives a list of `{name, type}` and returns `{log, error}`. Every middleware first logs `"<name>:in"`. Then, depending on `type`:

| type | behaviour |
|---|---|
| `"pass"` | calls `next()`, then logs `"<name>:out"` |
| `"stop"` | does **not** call `next()` (think: authentication failed); logs `"<name>:out"` |
| `"error"` | throws `Error("boom from <name>")` |
| `"catch"` | calls `next()` inside `try`/`catch`; if an error arrives logs `"<name>:caught <message>"`; then logs `"<name>:out"` |
| `"twice"` | calls `next()` two times, then logs `"<name>:out"` |

Calling `next()` from the last middleware runs the handler, which logs `"handler"`. A middleware's `next` may be called only once: a second call throws
`Error("next() called multiple times")`. An error that nobody catches unwinds the whole stack (skipped `:out` lines are simply not logged);
`error` is then its message, otherwise `null`.

**Example:** `[{name:"log",type:"pass"},{name:"auth",type:"pass"}]` → `{log:["log:in","auth:in","handler","auth:out","log:out"], error:null}`

guide.prereqs: Recursion, closures, `try`/`catch`. The lesson *Middleware and command*.
guide.intuition: Russian dolls. Opening doll 1 reveals doll 2, and so on to the centre (the handler); then each doll closes again in reverse order. `next()` means "open the next doll and come back to me when everything inside is finished".
hints: Write `dispatch(i)`: it runs middleware `i` and gives it a `next` that calls `dispatch(i + 1)`.
`dispatch(stack.length)` is the handler.
Give each `next` its own `called` flag (a closure variable) to detect a second call; let errors propagate as normal exceptions and catch them once at the top.
guide.brute_force: Two loops: forward for the `in` lines, backward for the `out` lines. It reproduces the happy path only; stop, errors and catching all depend on real nesting.
guide.approach:
Recursive dispatch.

**Dry run** `[guard:catch, a:pass, b:error, c:pass]`: `guard:in` → next → `a:in` → next → `b:in` → throws. The exception leaves `a` (no `a:out`) and is caught in `guard`: `guard:caught boom from b`, then `guard:out`. `error` is `null` because it was handled.
guide.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) call-stack depth for n middleware.
guide.pitfalls:
- Logging `:out` for a middleware an exception passed through.
- Sharing one `called` flag across all middleware.
- Forgetting that `stop` still logs its own `:out`.
guide.follow_up: Real Koa middleware is `async`: `await next()`. The dispatch function is the same with promises (see `koa-compose`).

node-command-undo.title: Commands with undo and redo
node-command-undo.description:
A to-do list starts empty. Every change is made through a **command object** that knows how to `run` itself and how to `undo` itself, which gives undo/redo for free.

| operation | effect |
|---|---|
| `["add", text]` | append `text` |
| `["remove", index]` | remove the item at `index` |
| `["set", index, text]` | replace the item at `index` |
| `["clear"]` | remove all items |
| `["undo"]` | reverse the most recent command that has not been undone; nothing happens if there is none |
| `["redo"]` | re-apply the most recently undone command; nothing happens if there is none |

Rules: `remove`/`set` with an index that is not a valid position are ignored completely (they do not enter the history).
Executing a **new** command (add/remove/set/clear) empties the redo history. `clear` on an empty list is still a command.

Return a list with a snapshot (copy) of the items after each operation.

**Example:** `[["add","milk"],["add","tea"],["undo"],["redo"],["remove",0],["undo"]]`
→ `[["milk"],["milk","tea"],["milk"],["milk","tea"],["tea"],["milk","tea"]]`

guide.prereqs: Stacks (`push`/`pop`), closures, `splice`. The lesson *Middleware and command*.
guide.intuition: Instead of doing a change directly, write it on a card that says both how to do it and how to reverse it. Done cards go on one pile; undo moves the top card to a second pile (after reversing it); redo moves it back. A fresh action throws the second pile away, because that future no longer exists.
hints: Two stacks: `undoStack` and `redoStack`, holding command objects with `run()` and `undo()`.
Each command factory captures what it needs to reverse itself (the removed item, the previous text, the cleared items).
Validate the index *before* creating the command; on a new command set `redoStack.length = 0`.
guide.brute_force: Save a full copy of the list before every change and restore copies on undo. Simple and correct, but O(n) memory per step; command objects store only the difference.
guide.approach:
Command objects plus two stacks.

**Dry run** on the example: `add milk`, `add tea` → undo stack `[addMilk, addTea]`. `undo` → addTea reversed → `[milk]`, redo stack `[addTea]`. `redo` → `[milk, tea]`. `remove 0` → remembers `milk`, list `[tea]`, redo cleared. `undo` → `milk` re-inserted at 0.
guide.complexity: O(1) per add/set/undo/redo of those; `remove` O(n) for the splice; `clear` O(n). Memory O(history size).
guide.pitfalls:
- Keeping the redo pile after a new command.
- Recording commands that did nothing because the index was invalid.
- Undoing `remove` by appending the item at the end instead of at its old index.
guide.follow_up: Serialise commands as plain data (`{type, args}`) and you can send them over the network or replay them later: the basis of job queues and event sourcing.

node-batch-cache.title: Request batching and caching
node-batch-cache.description:
An API server answers requests by key. Computing the answer for a key (a database query, say) takes `duration` ms. Two optimisations are layered on top:

- **Batching:** if a fetch for the same key is already in flight, a new request does not start another one; it waits for the running fetch and finishes when that fetch finishes.
- **Caching:** when a fetch completes at time `c`, its value stays valid for `ttl` ms: a request arriving at time `t` with `c <= t < c + ttl` is answered instantly from the cache.

`requests` is a list of `{t, key}` sorted by `t`. For each request return `{source, doneAt}` where `source` is `"fetch"` (it started a new fetch; done at `t + duration`),
`"batched"` (joined a fetch in flight; done when that fetch ends) or `"cache"` (done at `t`). Also return the number of fetches started.

A fetch started at `s` is in flight while `s <= t < s + duration`. Keys are independent of each other. `ttl` may be 0 (batching only).

**Example:** `duration = 100`, `ttl = 50`, requests for key `"a"` at t = 0, 30, 100, 149, 150
→ sources `fetch` (done 100), `batched` (100), `cache` (100), `cache` (149), `fetch` (250); `fetches = 2`.

guide.prereqs: `Map`, interval reasoning. The lesson *Async initialisation, request batching and caching*.
guide.intuition: Ten colleagues want the same report. The first one asks the archive; the other nine, seeing a request is already out, wait for that same copy (batching). For a while afterwards the copy on the desk is handed to anyone who asks (caching). Then it is considered stale and someone asks the archive again.
hints: Per key you only need one number: when the latest fetch started.
With `done = start + duration`, a request at `t` is batched if `t < done`, cached if `t < done + ttl`, otherwise it starts a new fetch.
Batched and cached requests do not change the stored start time.
guide.brute_force: For each request scan all earlier requests of the same key to find the latest fetch: O(n²). A map from key to the latest start makes it O(n).
guide.approach:
One pass with a `Map`.

**Dry run** on the example (duration 100, ttl 50): t=0 → fetch, start 0, done 100. t=30 → `30 < 100` → batched, done 100. t=100 → not `< 100`, but `< 150` → cache. t=149 → cache. t=150 → not `< 150` → new fetch, done 250.
guide.complexity: O(n) time, O(distinct keys) space.
guide.pitfalls:
- Starting the cache lifetime at the fetch's start.
- Off-by-one at the boundaries: at `t = done` the value is already cached; at `t = done + ttl` it has expired.
- Sharing state between keys.
guide.follow_up: In real code the map stores the **promise** of the running fetch: `if (running.has(key)) return running.get(key)`. Add error handling: a failed fetch must not be cached.

node-cancel-token.title: Cooperative cancellation
node-cancel-token.description:
An asynchronous operation runs `steps` one after another in virtual time, starting at 0. Each step is `{name, ms, abortable?}`.
Somebody may request cancellation at time `cancelAt` (`null` means never), as with `AbortController.abort()`.

JavaScript cannot interrupt running code from outside, so cancellation is **cooperative**:

1. Before starting each step the operation checks the cancel signal. If cancellation has been requested (`now >= cancelAt`), it stops there.
2. A normal step, once started, always runs to its end, even if the cancel request arrives in the middle.
3. An **abortable** step (one that was handed the signal, like `fetch(url, {signal})`) is interrupted at the instant of the request: if `cancelAt` is before the step's end, the operation ends at `cancelAt` and the step does not count as completed.
4. After the last step finishes the operation is done; a cancel request arriving at that moment or later has no effect.

Return `{completed, status, endedAt}` where `completed` lists the names of the finished steps and `status` is `"done"` or `"cancelled"`.

**Example:** steps `read 10ms`, `parse 20ms`, `upload 50ms (abortable)`, `cancelAt = 40` → `{completed:["read","parse"], status:"cancelled", endedAt:40}`.
With `cancelAt = 15` → `{completed:["read","parse"], status:"cancelled", endedAt:30}` (parse was already running and is not abortable).

guide.prereqs: Loops, early `return`. The lesson *Cancelling async work and running CPU-bound tasks*.
guide.intuition: A cook following a recipe who glances at the "order cancelled" light only between steps. Chopping, once begun, is finished; but the oven has its own off switch wired to the light, so baking stops the moment the light comes on.
hints: Walk through the steps with a clock `now`.
At the top of each iteration: if `cancelAt !== null && now >= cancelAt`, return cancelled at `now`.
For an abortable step compare `cancelAt` with the step's end time: if it is earlier, return cancelled at `cancelAt`.
guide.brute_force: Advance the clock 1 ms at a time, checking the signal each millisecond: O(total duration) and easy to get the boundaries wrong.
guide.approach:
Check, then run.

**Dry run** (`cancelAt = 15`): before `read`, `0 >= 15` is false → run to 10. Before `parse`, `10 >= 15` false → it starts; not abortable → runs to 30. Before `upload`, `30 >= 15` → cancelled at 30 with `[read, parse]` completed.
guide.complexity: O(number of steps).
guide.pitfalls:
- Interrupting ordinary steps mid-way: plain promises cannot be stopped from outside.
- Treating `cancelAt = 0` as "no cancellation" because `0` is falsy; compare with `null`.
- Reporting `cancelled` when the request arrives after everything has finished.
guide.follow_up: Add a `cleanup` duration per completed step that runs in reverse order after cancellation (closing files, rolling back), as a `finally` block would.

node-lru-cache.title: A bounded LRU cache
node-lru-cache.description:
An in-memory cache without a size limit is one of the most common memory leaks in Node.js services. Implement a cache that holds at most `capacity` (≥ 1) entries and,
when full, evicts the **least recently used** one. Both reading and writing a key count as using it.

`runLru(capacity, ops)` returns one result per operation:

| operation | result |
|---|---|
| `["get", key]` | the value, or `-1` if absent (a hit makes the key the most recently used) |
| `["put", key, value]` | inserts or updates and makes the key the most recently used. Result: the key that had to be evicted, or `null` |
| `["keys"]` | the keys from least to most recently used |

**Example:** `capacity = 2`, ops `[["put","a",1],["put","b",2],["get","a"],["put","c",3],["get","b"],["keys"]]` → `[null, null, 1, "b", -1, ["a","c"]]`

guide.prereqs: `Map` and the fact that it iterates in insertion order. The lesson *Interview essentials* (memory leaks).
guide.intuition: A small desk with room for a few books. Each time you use a book you put it back on the right-hand end. When the desk is full and a new book arrives, the book at the far left, untouched the longest, goes back to the shelf.
hints: A JavaScript `Map` remembers insertion order: the first key it yields is the oldest inserted.
To mark a key as recently used, delete it and set it again.
On `put` of a new key into a full cache, evict `map.keys().next().value` first.
guide.brute_force: An array of `[key, value]` pairs with a linear search and `splice` on every access: O(n) per operation.
guide.approach:
Map as an ordered dictionary.

**Dry run** on the example: put a, put b → order `a, b`. `get a` → 1, order `b, a`. `put c` → full, evict `b` → order `a, c`. `get b` → -1. `keys` → `[a, c]`.
guide.complexity: O(1) average per `get`/`put`; `keys` is O(n). Space O(capacity).
guide.pitfalls:
- Forgetting that `get` refreshes recency (that gives FIFO, not LRU).
- Evicting when updating an existing key.
- `if (map.get(key))` fails for stored values `0`, `""` or `false`; use `has`.
guide.follow_up: Add a time-to-live per entry. The classic interview version asks for a doubly linked list plus a hash map; explain why `Map` gives the same complexity.

node-round-robin.title: Round-robin load balancer with failing workers
node-round-robin.description:
A load balancer spreads requests over `workers` (a fixed list of distinct names, in order) using **round robin**, skipping workers that are currently down.

It keeps a `pointer`, an index into the full list, starting at 0. For a request it examines the workers starting at `pointer` and moving forward (wrapping around),
picks the first one that is up, and sets `pointer` to the position just after the chosen worker. If every worker is down the request cannot be served.

`events` is a list of `["req"]`, `["down", name]` and `["up", name]`. Return one result per event: the chosen worker name for a request (`null` if none is up), and `null` for `down`/`up`.
All workers start up. `down` on a worker that is already down, or `up` on one that is up, changes nothing.

**Example:** workers `["w1","w2","w3"]`, events `req, req, down w3, req, req, up w3, req`
→ `["w1","w2",null,"w1","w2",null,"w3"]`

guide.prereqs: Modulo arithmetic, `Set`. The lesson *The scale cube, cluster and zero-downtime restarts*.
guide.intuition: Dealing cards around a table. If a player has left their seat you skip them and deal to the next person who is present; the next card continues from there.
hints: Keep a `Set` of down workers and an integer `pointer`.
For a request, try at most `workers.length` positions: `(pointer + step) % workers.length`.
After choosing index `i`, set `pointer = (i + 1) % workers.length`.
guide.brute_force: Filter the healthy workers and index with a request counter modulo their count. The distribution jumps whenever a worker fails or returns, and some workers get two requests in a row.
guide.approach:
Pointer over the full list.

**Dry run** on the example: req → w1 (pointer 1). req → w2 (pointer 2). w3 down. req → index 2 is down, wrap to 0 → w1 (pointer 1). req → w2 (pointer 2). w3 up. req → w3 (pointer 0).
guide.complexity: O(n) per request in the worst case (all but one down), O(1) typically; O(n) space.
guide.pitfalls:
- Dividing by zero or looping forever when all workers are down.
- Advancing the pointer by one rather than to just past the chosen worker.
- An empty worker list.
guide.follow_up: Implement *least connections* (pick the worker with the fewest requests in flight) and compare the fairness when request durations vary.

node-consistent-hash.title: Consistent hashing ring
node-consistent-hash.description:
To decide which server stores a key (a cache shard, a sticky session), `hash(key) % numberOfServers` works until a server is added or removed: then almost every key moves.
**Consistent hashing** moves only a small share of the keys.

Use this 32-bit hash (FNV-1a) exactly:

```
h = 2166136261
for each character c of the text:  h = h XOR charCode(c);  h = (h * 16777619) mod 2^32     // in JS: Math.imul(h, 16777619) >>> 0
```

The ring: every node contributes `replicas` points, the hashes of the labels `"<node>#0"`, `"<node>#1"`, … `"<node>#<replicas-1>"`.
A key belongs to the node owning the first point whose hash is `>= hash(key)`; if there is none, wrap around to the point with the smallest hash.
(If two points have the same hash, the one with the alphabetically smaller label comes first.)

`consistentHash(replicas, ops)` processes `["add", node]`, `["remove", node]` and `["get", key]` and returns one result per operation: the owning node for `get`
(`null` if the ring is empty) and `null` for `add`/`remove`. Adding a node twice or removing an unknown node changes nothing.

**Example:** `consistentHash(3, [["add","A"],["add","B"],["get","user:1"],["remove","A"],["get","user:1"]])` → a list of five results where the last is `"B"` (the only node left).

guide.prereqs: Sorting, binary search, bitwise operators (`^`, `>>> 0`, `Math.imul`). The lesson *Reverse proxies, service discovery and microservices*.
guide.intuition: Seat the servers around a round table at positions given by a hash. A key also gets a position and walks clockwise to the first server it meets. If a server leaves, only the keys that were walking to it continue to the next one; everybody else stays put. Several seats per server (replicas) even out the gaps.
hints: Implement the hash exactly; `Math.imul` does 32-bit multiplication and `>>> 0` makes the result unsigned.
Keep the ring as an array of `{hash, label, node}` sorted by hash; rebuild or re-sort when a node is added.
For `get`, binary-search the first point with `hash >= h`; if the search runs off the end, use index 0.
guide.brute_force: For each `get`, scan every point and keep the smallest hash that is `>= h`: O(points) per lookup. Sorting once and binary searching gives O(log points).
guide.approach:
Sorted ring plus binary search.

**Dry run** in words (`replicas = 3`, nodes A and B): the ring has six points. `get user:1` hashes the key and finds the next point clockwise; say it belongs to A. After `remove A` only B's three points remain, so the same walk now ends at a B point: the answer becomes `B`. Keys that already belonged to B are unaffected.
guide.complexity: `add` O(P log P) for P points on the ring; `remove` O(P); `get` O(log P + key length).
guide.pitfalls:
- Leaving the hash signed (negative numbers sort before positive ones and the ring order changes).
- Forgetting the wrap-around.
- Using `hash % nodes`, which is the thing being replaced.
- Adding a node twice and doubling its points.
guide.follow_up: Measure it: with 4 nodes and 1,000 keys, how many keys change owner when a fifth node joins? Compare with modulo hashing (about 80%).

node-pubsub-broker.title: A pub/sub broker with topic wildcards
node-pubsub-broker.description:
Build a small message **broker**. Publishers send a message to a *topic* such as `orders.eu.created` (words separated by dots). Subscribers register *patterns*:

- a word matches itself;
- `*` matches **exactly one** word;
- `#` matches **zero or more** words.

So `orders.*.created` matches `orders.eu.created` but not `orders.created`; `orders.#` matches `orders`, `orders.eu` and `orders.eu.created`; `#` matches everything.

Operations:

| operation | effect |
|---|---|
| `["sub", client, pattern]` | the client subscribes to the pattern (repeating the same subscription changes nothing) |
| `["unsub", client, pattern]` | removes that exact subscription if present |
| `["pub", topic, message]` | delivers `message` to every client with at least one matching pattern. A client receives a message **once**, even if several of its patterns match |

Return `{deliveries, inbox}`: `deliveries` has one entry per `pub`, the alphabetically sorted list of clients that received it; `inbox` maps every client that ever
subscribed to the list of messages it received, in order. Messages published before a client subscribes are not delivered later.

**Example:** `[["sub","ann","orders.*"],["sub","bob","#"],["pub","orders.new","m1"],["pub","users.new","m2"]]`
→ `{deliveries:[["ann","bob"],["bob"]], inbox:{ann:["m1"], bob:["m1","m2"]}}`

guide.prereqs: `Map`, `Set`, recursion on arrays. The lesson *Messaging fundamentals and publish/subscribe*.
guide.intuition: A newspaper kiosk: readers leave standing orders ("anything about sport", "local news only"), and each new issue goes to everyone whose order fits, without the journalist knowing who they are. The interesting part is deciding whether an order fits a topic, word by word.
hints: Split both pattern and topic on `.` and compare the word lists recursively.
Cases for the first pattern word: an ordinary word or `*` consumes exactly one topic word; `#` may consume 0, 1, 2, … words, so try each possibility.
Store subscriptions as `Map<client, Set<pattern>>`; on publish use `some` over a client's patterns so the message is pushed once.
guide.brute_force: Translate each pattern to a regular expression (`*` → `[^.]+`, `#` → `.*`). It works but the zero-word case of `#` next to dots is fiddly (`a.#` must match `a`).
guide.approach:
`matches(pattern, topic)`: empty pattern matches only an empty topic; `#` loops over how many words to skip; otherwise compare one word and recurse.

**Dry run** `a.#.z` against `a.z`: `a` = `a`; then `#` tries to skip 0 words: remaining pattern `[z]` vs topic `[z]` → match. Against `a.b.c`: `#` skips 0, 1 or 2 words and `z` never lines up → no match.
guide.complexity: Matching is O(p·t) with memoisation (exponential worst case without it, harmless for short topics). A publish costs O(total subscriptions).
guide.pitfalls:
- `#` must be able to match zero words.
- A client with several matching patterns receiving duplicates.
- Delivering old messages to new subscribers; plain pub/sub has no memory.
guide.follow_up: Real brokers store patterns in a trie so a publish does not test every subscription. Add *durable* subscribers that receive what they missed while offline.

node-work-queue.title: A work queue with acknowledgements
node-work-queue.description:
A **work queue** hands each message to exactly one of several competing workers and keeps it until the worker confirms it is done.

State: a FIFO list of *ready* messages; the set of joined workers; for each worker at most **one** unacknowledged message (prefetch = 1); and a line of idle workers ordered by how long they have been idle.

Operations (after **every** operation run *dispatch*: while there is a ready message and an idle worker, give the oldest ready message to the worker at the head of the idle line and record `[worker, message]` in `deliveries`):

| operation | effect |
|---|---|
| `["send", message]` | append the message to the ready list |
| `["join", worker]` | a new worker joins at the back of the idle line (ignored if already joined) |
| `["ack", worker, message]` | valid only if the worker currently holds exactly that message: the message is finished (append to `acked`) and the worker goes to the back of the idle line. Otherwise ignored |
| `["nack", worker, message]` | valid under the same condition: the worker goes to the back of the idle line and the message returns to the **front** of the ready list |
| `["leave", worker]` | the worker disconnects (ignored if unknown). If it held a message, that message returns to the front of the ready list |

Return `{deliveries, ready, unacked, acked}`: all deliveries in order, the messages still ready, an object mapping each busy worker to the message it holds, and acknowledged messages in order.
Messages are distinct strings.

**Example:** `[["send","m1"],["send","m2"],["join","w1"],["join","w2"],["nack","w1","m1"],["ack","w2","m2"]]`
→ deliveries `[["w1","m1"],["w2","m2"],["w1","m1"]]`, ready `[]`, unacked `{w1:"m1"}`, acked `["m2"]`.

guide.prereqs: Queues, `Map`, `Set`. The lesson *Task queues, competing consumers and request/reply*.
guide.intuition: A taxi rank. Passengers (messages) queue on one side, free taxis (workers) on the other; the first passenger takes the first taxi. The dispatcher crosses a passenger off the list only when the driver radios "delivered" (ack). If the taxi breaks down, the passenger goes back to the front of the line.
hints: Four structures: `ready` (array), `idle` (array of workers), `holding` (`Map` worker → message), `members` (`Set`).
Write `dispatch()` once and call it after every operation.
For `ack`/`nack`, first check `holding.get(worker) === message`; then free the worker (push to `idle`) and either record the ack or `unshift` the message.
guide.brute_force: Recompute who is idle by scanning all workers each time. It works but loses the "longest idle first" order unless you also track timestamps; an explicit idle line is simpler.
guide.approach:
State machine plus dispatch.

**Dry run** on the example: two sends → ready `[m1, m2]`. `join w1` → dispatch gives `m1` to w1. `join w2` → `m2` to w2. `nack w1 m1` → w1 idle, `m1` at the front of ready → dispatch gives `m1` to w1 again. `ack w2 m2` → acked `[m2]`, w2 idle, nothing ready.
guide.complexity: O(1) amortised per operation apart from `unshift`/`splice` on arrays (O(n)); fine at this scale, a deque would make them O(1).
guide.pitfalls:
- Deleting a message at delivery time (that is *at-most-once*: a crash loses work).
- Accepting an ack from a worker that does not hold the message.
- Forgetting to remove a leaving idle worker from the idle line, so it gets a message after it has gone.
guide.follow_up: Add a delivery counter per message and move it to a *dead-letter* list after three nacks, so a poisonous message cannot loop forever.

node-request-reply.title: Request/reply with correlation ids

guide.prereqs: `Map`, sorting with two keys. The lesson *Task queues, competing consumers and request/reply*.
guide.intuition: A cloakroom. You hand over a coat and get a numbered ticket; coats come back in any order and the number tells which coat is whose. A ticket nobody issued, a ticket used twice and a ticket presented after closing time are the three ways it goes wrong.
hints: Store each request in a `Map` under its id with its expiry time and a state.
For a reply, test the four cases in the order given in the statement.
At the end, every request whose state is not `resolved` is timed out; sort those by `(expires, id)`.
guide.brute_force: For each reply, search the whole event list backwards for the matching request: O(n²). The map makes each reply O(1).
guide.approach:
One pass, then a filter and sort.

**Dry run** on the example: `r1` expires at 50, `r2` at 15. Reply for `r2` at 20: `20 >= 15` → late. Reply for `r1` at 30 → resolved `A`. Second reply for `r1` → duplicate. Reply for `r9` → unknown. Unresolved: `r2`.
guide.complexity: O(n log n) because of the final sort; O(n) space.
guide.pitfalls:
- Resolving a request with a reply that came after its timeout (the caller has already been told it failed).
- Using `>` instead of `>=` at the deadline.
- Forgetting requests that never got any reply.
guide.follow_up: In real code each pending entry holds the promise's `resolve`/`reject` and a timer that deletes the entry; forgetting the deletion is a memory leak.
